items.label: text
items.text: Why aren't ion charges shown in formulae? Actually, they can be shown. For example, the formula for sodium chloride is NaCl. It is sometimes written Na+Cl- if you are trying to make a particular point, but for most purposes the charges are left out. In an ionic compound, the charges are there, whether you write them or not.

items.label: section_header
items.text: To find the formula for iron(Ill) sulfate

items.label: text
items.text: Iron(III) tells you that the metal ion is Fe3+.

items.label: text
items.text: To have equal numbers of positive and negative charges, you would need two iron(Ill) ions for every three sulfate ions, giving 6+ and 6– in total.

items.label: text
items.text: A shortcut to working out complicated formulae such as these is to just swap over the numbers in the charges. This is shown in Figure 7.13.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 7.13 If you cross over the numbers in the charges you will get the formula.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 7.14 To work out the formula of calcium chloride we cross over the numbers in the charges. There is no extra number in front of the charge in Cl- because we do not tend to write in a 1.

items.label: text
items.text: You have to be careful using this method because you can get the wrong answer when the charges on the ions are the same. For example, the formula of calcium oxide is CaO and not Ca2O2. When the charges on the positive and negative ions are the same you can deduce that there will be 1 of each ion in the formula, so there is no need to swap anything over.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 7.15 The formula of calcium oxide is Ca0 and not Ca2O2.

items.label: text
items.text: All ionic compounds form crystals that consist of lattices of positive and negative ions packed together in a regular way. A lattice is a regular array of particles. The lattice is held together by the strong electrostatic attractions between the positively and negatively charged ions.

items.label: caption
items.text: Figure 7.16 A lattice fence. A lattice is a regular, repeating structure.
